Discipline as Consistency with Disliked Tasks

frameworks.name: Rule of 300 (Warm Outreach Breakdown)
frameworks.definition: A three-step decomposition of the Rule of 100 for warm outreach: (1) post one piece of content on one platform, (2) leave 100 high-quality comments inside a community of your target audience, (3) do one-on-one outreach to the warm list generated by step 2 (post likers, post commenters, comment likers, comment repliers).

frameworks.name: Four-Stage Customer Acquisition Sequence (Homies to Paid)
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's personal framework for getting first customers: Stage 1 (Homies) - train friends for free to collect before/afters; Stage 2 (Referrals) - ask those friends to refer others; Stage 3 (Charitable Bridge) - accept donations-to-charity in lieu of cash to overcome pricing fear; Stage 4 (Paid Launch) - convert existing network to paid using accumulated proof.

frameworks.name: 13 Instructions for Starting Entrepreneurs
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's Slack message (seen by ~4 million people) listing 13 operating rules for new entrepreneurs: follow instructions, Google before asking, share what you learn, do the Rule of 100 daily, expect excitement to fade before real work starts, recognize you are the product being built, accept that everything is unscalable at first, understand pain forces improvement, eliminate complaining, repeat proven actions, write down your reasons, accept that hard = consistency not complexity, and just win once to get addicted.
frameworks.concept: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that proof beats promise: a seller with 100 pieces of documented proof and a mediocre offer will outperform a seller with an excellent offer but no proof, because prospects require evidence similar to their own situation before believing a result is achievable for them.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospects are evaluating a new service provider
no strong referral or brand exists
claims.mechanism: Prospects pattern-match their avatar to existing proof; if they see someone like themselves who succeeded, the cognitive leap to believing it will work for them is minimized.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that referrals are worth more per lead than any other lead source for three compounding reasons: they convert at higher rates, they close at higher prices, and referred customers are themselves more likely to refer others - meaning the referral flywheel amplifies its own value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: referrals are the most important type of marketing
conditions: early-stage service business
founder has no significant audience or paid advertising
claims.mechanism: Referrals arrive with pre-existing social trust, reducing objection surface and enabling higher price acceptance; their social network then shares that same trust baseline, perpetuating the cycle.
bounded_by: If a founder is not getting referrals, Hormozi interprets this as a quality signal - meaning the underlying service is not good enough, so pouring more advertising into the funnel would amplify a bad product.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that non-monetary compensation from early free clients (testimonials, feedback, referrals) is worth more than whatever cash a founder could have charged, because a single strong testimonial will produce more downstream revenue over the long term than the foregone fee.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has zero existing proof or track record
early-stage, pre-revenue or pre-scale phase
claims.mechanism: A strong testimonial functions as an ongoing acquisition asset reused across every future sales conversation; the cash that could have been charged is a one-time transaction, whereas proof compounds.
bounded_by: Hormozi notes he stayed free longer than necessary, suggesting this logic has a ceiling; once sufficient proof exists the founder should move to paid.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi uses a strict full-price-or-free pricing policy with no discounting: he either charges full price or delivers for free in exchange for testimonials, referrals, and feedback, and never makes individual price exceptions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any service business regardless of stage
claims.mechanism: Discounting to close an individual deal communicates to that buyer and everyone they tell that prices are negotiable and not real; this turns every future sales conversation into a haggle and permanently degrades perceived value.
bounded_by: A founder can make a strategic decision to lower prices permanently, which is different from one-off exceptions for individual buyers.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that niching down into a specific avatar (e.g., skinny-to-swole male fitness) both increases the value delivered to each client and decreases the cost to serve them, because templated solutions become far more precise when everyone shares the same starting point and goal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business
founder doing delivery personally
claims.mechanism: With a homogeneous avatar, the founder's solution templates can be built once to very high depth rather than generically built for each person; depth of solution at the same or lower time cost produces more client results, which in turn generates more proof and referrals.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that failing to build a next offer for existing customers - and instead going to find all-new customers after a program ends - is the single largest recoverable revenue mistake in early service businesses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business with a finite-length program (e.g., 12-week package)
customers who completed the program and got results
claims.mechanism: Customers who completed and succeeded already trust the provider and want more of the same result; re-acquiring an already-converted customer costs zero, whereas finding a new customer requires re-running the full acquisition process.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that maintaining a low personal burn rate early in a business (he lived on $1,200 per month while earning a consulting salary and saved approximately $50,000 after taxes over two years) was the enabling condition for leaving employment and going all-in - because financial runway extended the time horizon on which bets could be placed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: pre-launch phase before full-time business commitment
founder still employed with income
claims.mechanism: Savings rate converts income into runway; runway converts urgency from monthly to multi-year; multi-year urgency allows the founder to take larger bets and absorb longer feedback loops without needing immediate revenue to survive.

numbers.axis: monthly personal burn rate vs. income

anchors.region: savings accumulated over 2 years post-tax on consulting income

anchors.value: 2-3 years at the same burn rate

bounded_by: Hormozi notes saving money alone does not make money - it only buys time to take risks.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that working more is the highest-leverage savings mechanism because it simultaneously generates income and eliminates the free time in which money would otherwise be spent.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: biggest hack of all for saving money is to work more
conditions: early-stage founder with access to additional working time
discretionary spending is lifestyle-driven rather than necessity-driven
claims.mechanism: Working more creates income on the upside and eliminates idle time on the downside; both effects compound the savings rate multiplicatively rather than additively.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that online service businesses are the easiest first business to start because they require near-zero capital to launch, have low recurring overhead, can be operated from anywhere, and the founder learns all fundamental business mistakes on a low-stakes vehicle before encountering them in a capital-intensive model.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: starting an online service business is the easiest one to start
conditions: first business for a founder with no prior track record
founder has access to the internet
bounded_by: Hormozi distinguishes this from brick-and-mortar businesses which require capital, leases, and have much higher failure cost from early mistakes.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that consistency of inputs determines consistency of outputs in a business: if you send 10 outreaches per day you will see one sale every 10 days (which feels volatile) but if you send 100 outreaches per day you will see roughly one sale per day (which feels stable) - the volatility is a function of input volume, not channel quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.topic: Discipline as Consistency with Disliked Tasks
conditions: early-stage founder using warm/cold outreach as primary acquisition channel
claims.mechanism: A sales channel's average conversion ratio is fixed in the short term; the variance around each period's output scales inversely with input volume - 10 inputs yields one expected output with high variance, 100 inputs yields one expected output per day with low variance.

numbers.axis: daily outreach volume vs. perceived output stability

anchors.value: ~1 sale per 10 days (high variance, feels volatile)
~1 sale per day (lower variance, feels consistent)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that real work begins only when initial excitement fades, and that activity done while excited does not count as work in any meaningful sense - because the test of a founder is whether they perform the same actions after the novelty is gone.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.topic: The Execution Gap: Knowledge Without Action
conditions: early-stage entrepreneurs in the first weeks of a new business or project

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that pain from repetitive low-result activity (like sending 100 outreaches and getting few replies) is the catalyst for skill development, because pain motivates the founder to find a better method; finding the better method is how leverage is gained.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: pain of repetition is what forces you to seek improvement
conditions: founder using any high-volume repetitive acquisition or production activity
claims.mechanism: Pain from low conversion signals inefficiency; the discomfort forces experimentation and iteration; the resulting improvement produces higher output per unit of effort - which is the operational definition of leverage.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the ability to work for a long period without receiving results is itself a durable competitive advantage, because a competitor who requires immediate reward will quit before a competitor who can sustain effort for a year without visible output - and the latter will compound past the former by the time results appear.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any high-volume, long-feedback-cycle business skill

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that complaining is a learned behavior reinforced by attention and affection from others, and therefore functionally transfers the speaker's positioning from enviable to pitiable - reducing the social status and peer caliber of their environment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: if you complain, you are dead to me
claims.mechanism: Complaining is historically rewarded with attention, affection, and sympathy; those rewards condition repetition of the behavior; but the social command given by complaining is 'pity me,' which positions the speaker as low-status rather than high-status or aspirational.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when someone executes all the documented steps of a proven process but still fails to get the same outcome, the problem is an unidentified variable in their execution - not that the process does not work - and the correct response is to study the discrepancy rather than declare the approach broken.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founders following a documented, proven acquisition or business process

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a founder stopping a working online business (making $4,000/month with only four hours per week of effort in 2013) to chase a perceived-more-legitimate brick-and-mortar business was a major mistake, because the correct response was to scale the working model rather than abandon it for something unfamiliar.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder has a working, profitable model
founder is tempted by a perceived-more-legitimate alternative

numbers.axis: effort vs. revenue in the abandoned online fitness business circa 2013

anchors.region: implied ceiling if effort matched 40 hrs/week

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that fear of social judgment - specifically what classmates and his father would think of an online business - was a primary driver keeping him underpaid for years, because major life decisions were made on the basis of imagined opinions of people who were not thinking about him at all.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage founders from traditional educational or professional backgrounds
claims.mechanism: Imagined social judgment generates phantom downside (embarrassment, disapproval) that is weighted against real upside (income, freedom); when that phantom downside is large enough it prevents action regardless of objective economics.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that comments made inside a niche community on someone else's high-performing content get substantially more reach than original content posted from a zero-audience account, because the comment piggybacks on the distribution the original post already has.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: almost like you running mini ads
conditions: founder with zero or near-zero existing audience
commenting inside a community or group where target customers congregate
claims.mechanism: A comment inside a community surfaces to everyone who views the parent post; within those viewers, the comment competes only against other comments on that same post rather than all content on the platform - making it easier to appear prominently despite having no distribution of one's own.
bounded_by: Comments that pitch or self-promote are likely to be blocked by the community owner and damage reputation.

examples.text: After training friends for free and gathering before-and-after transformation pictures, Alex Hormozi launched the Skinny to Swole paid program at $200 per month for 12 weeks. He reached out to everyone he knew with all accumulated testimonials from the prior three stages, converted 20 paying clients, and generated $4,000 per month in profit - his first $12,000 total - entirely from warm outreach and documented proof, with no paid advertising and no formal offer structure.

When Alex Hormozi first asked the free-training clients to refer friends without any financial commitment required, many of those referred friends agreed but then did nothing because they had no skin in the game. He solved this by introducing the Free Training Project structure: referred clients donated $500-$1,000 to a charity of their choice, giving them enough commitment to actually participate while still allowing Hormozi to frame the training as free (they were paying the charity, not him).

In the Skinny to Swole program Alex Hormozi sold 20 clients on 12-week packages at $200 per month. When the 12 weeks ended, he went looking for new clients instead of offering existing clients a continuation or next program. He later identified this as a major mistake: every client who got results had an unsatisfied appetite for more progress (e.g., a guy who added 30 pounds to his bench press did not want to stop), and Hormozi left all of that expansion revenue on the table by not having a second offer ready.

Sandy Smith, a woman Alex Hormozi met at his local gym, asked him to advise her on nutrition and suggested they meet at a pizza shop. After an hour and a half conversation covering food substitutions and protein targets, she reached into her purse and wrote him a $100 check. Hormozi describes this as his first light-bulb moment - the realization that he could make money from something he genuinely loved doing - which became the catalyst for starting a formal fitness business.

Alex Hormozi describes building an Excel spreadsheet that took approximately 200 hours to create: a tool that, given a client's weight and goal, automatically calculated macros and generated a customized grocery list and meal plan drawn from 100 meal options. Once built, completing a new client's plan required only about 10 minutes. He would deliberately delay sending it by a week so it appeared as though each plan was custom-built from scratch - creating the perception of enormous personalized effort at a tiny marginal cost per client.

Alex Hormozi's first public content post (made approximately one year into his free training work) read: 'For the better part of a year I've been taking part in a free personal training project... I currently have a few slots on my roster. Drop me a note quickly if you're interested.' This post, combined with embedded transformation images, generated approximately 20 paying clients for his Skinny to Swole launch. He notes in retrospect that a stronger version would have led with the images directly, included a clear offer, added bonuses and risk reversal, and created scarcity - but even the weak version worked because of the accumulated proof behind it.

practices.text: Start by training friends and family for free in exchange for before-and-after documentation before approaching any paying strangers.
After delivering results to your first free clients, ask them specifically to send referrals who have already seen their transformation - do not ask for referrals before results are visible.
Apply the Rule of 100 daily: 100 warm outreaches, or 100 cold prospect contacts, or 100 minutes making and posting content, or $100/day in ads - pick one and execute it every day.
When making comments in online communities, always write a thoughtful substantive response to the post rather than a one-word reaction; the goal is to make the single best comment in that thread.

After someone likes your post, comments on your post, likes your comment, or replies to your comment, initiate a direct one-on-one outreach referencing their specific action as the conversation opener.
Price your service at either full price or free with explicit non-monetary compensation expectations; never discount to win an individual deal.
Write down every reason you will stick with your business, post the list where you will see it during daily repetitive work, and revisit it when motivation fades.
Before scaling or switching to a new business, ask: what would happen if I just worked 10x more hours on this exact model at the same conversion rate?
Always have a next offer prepared before the current program ends so existing customers can ascend without a gap.
Google any friction point or unknown before posting a question to a community or mentor; treat the Google search as the first mandatory step before escalating.
